newsitem.title: USA: States cracking down on teenage smoking.
newsitem.headline: States cracking down on teenage smoking.

text.p: Most U.S. states took steps last year to crack down on tobacco use, particularly teenage smoking, according to a survey released Wednesday.
The survey by the American Lung Association and other health groups found that states passed new laws and ballot initiatives, raised taxes and increased penalties for selling to minors.
Massachusetts went even further, passing a law that would require tobacco manufacturers to disclose all the ingredients in their products.
The national average for state excise taxes on cigarettes is now 33.2 cents per pack. Taxes range from 82.5 cents per pack in Washington D.C., to 2.5 percent in Virginia.
All 50 states and Washington have banned cigarette sales to minors. Most states define that as anyone under 18 although a few set older age limits.

Last Friday federal regulations went into effect banning sales to anyone under age 18, and requiring photo I.D. checks of anyone under 27. Other federal regulations restricting advertising, vending machines and tobacco sponsorship of entertainment or sporting events will be phased in over the next 18 months, if they survive a court challenge.

Teen smoking rates have been on the rise for the past few years and the new federal regulations aim at cutting the rate in half over seven years. About 3,000 teens start smoking each day, and health experts estimate that one-third of them will eventually die of smoking-related diseases such as lung cancer.
